title: Fsync latency causing failed liveness/readiness probes and scheduler backpressure - retro
body:
Summary:

On 2025-02-14 (US-WEST), we observed a widespread increase in pod restarts and prolonged pod Pending phases across two clusters (prod-west-1a, prod-west-1b). Symptoms were failed liveness/readiness probes (HTTP 502 / TCP timeout) on multiple stateful workloads and a spike in scheduling latency leading to backlog and autoscaler thrash.

Impact:
- ~12% of user-facing frontend pods restarted during the 20-minute spike.
- Several stateful worker StatefulSets experienced slow volume attaches and intermittent crashloops.
- Controller-manager and kube-scheduler latencies increased; median scheduling latency climbed from ~60ms to ~850ms for 15 minutes.
- Customer-facing error rate rose ~4x during the event window.

High-level cause hypothesis:
- Root cause appears to be large fsync/flush latency on nodes' local ephemeral disks (nvme-backed ephemeral volumes). Processes waiting on writes caused pod process stalls; probes timed out and Kubernetes killed/restarted pods. The resulting churn increased control-plane pressure and triggered scheduling/backpressure effects.

Why this manifested as a cluster-wide issue:
- Many pods use aggressive liveness/readiness probe timeouts (initialDelaySeconds=5, periodSeconds=10, timeoutSeconds=1). When fsync stalls for >1s, probes mark pods unhealthy.
- Nodes reporting multiple pod restarts pushed kubelet event churn to apiserver; watch/event backlog increased and scheduler work queues grew.
- Autoscaler reacted to Pending pods by requesting nodes; cloud provider attach/detach APIs hit rate limits, further delaying remediation.

Timeline (reconstructed):
- 2025-02-14T10:07:23Z: First observability alert — pod restart rate alarm for prod-west-1a (pager to oncall SRE).
- 10:08—10:13: Multiple Liveness/Readiness probe failures across 27 pods (frontend + workers).
- 10:09: Kubelet logs on node i-0ab3 show repeated fsync latency warnings (fsync took 2.3s, 4.1s).
- 10:11: APIServer watch latency increased; control-plane error budget alert fires.
- 10:12: Autoscaler scales up; new nodes take longer than expected due to attach timeouts.
- 10:27: Underlying disk vendor reports intermittent firmware background write flushing tied to GC/firmware-level encryption cycle in certain NVMe families.
- 10:35: Mitigations applied (see below). Metrics returned to baseline by 10:50.

Investigation artifacts and key logs (high level):
- kubelet logs: repeated "disk sync took Xms" / "fsync latency" entries; stacktraces show create/write path blocked in sync_file_range/fsync in container processes.
- dmesg on nodes: block layer timeout warnings followed by kernel writeback stall warnings.
- Cloud provider volume attach logs: increased attach latency for new ephemeral volumes while autoscaler requested nodes.
- App-level traces: HTTP handlers blocked during sync windows; p95 response time spiked.

Immediate mitigations performed during incident:
1) Increased liveness/readiness probe timeout for high-risk Deployments and StatefulSets (temporarily set timeoutSeconds=5, initialDelaySeconds=15) to reduce accidental restarts. Commands used:
   kubectl -n frontend patch deployment frontend --type='json' -p='[ {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/timeoutSeconds", "value": 5 } ]'
2) Disabled aggressive syncfs in a small Canary node pool by setting sysctl options (vm.dirty_expire_centisecs increased) to relax immediate sync pressure on kernel writeback.
3) Placed nodes from affected NVMe family into maintenance (drain with --ignore-daemonsets, cordon) and replaced with alternative instance types.
4) Adjusted cluster-autoscaler cooldown to 10m to avoid rapid scale flips while recovery ongoing.

Short-term outcome:
- Probe timeouts stopped triggering after increasing probe timeouts and draining worst nodes.
- Control-plane work queues cleared in ~20–30 minutes after node replacements and autoscaler cooldown.

Root cause analysis (detailed):
- Primary trigger: firmware-level background flush behavior on a subset of NVMe devices we used for ephemeral /var/lib/kubelet volumes. These devices entered periodic long-blocking flushes during heavy write patterns (observed during scheduled log rotation + checkpoint flushes).
- Secondary contributors:
  - Aggressive liveness/readiness probe settings made short blocking periods visible as failures.
  - Some application processes call fsync frequently (to meet durability semantics), amplifying contention.
  - Autoscaler and attach/detach plumbing exposed rate limits in the cloud provider when many pods cycled simultaneously.

Permanent mitigations and action items (owner, ETA):
- (Samir Gupta) Replace affected instance families in prod-west with newer NVMe firmware images or different instance types; phased roll by 2025-03-07.
- (Owen Patel) Update default liveness/readiness probe recommendation docs and a preflight check in deployment linting to warn about very low timeoutSeconds. ETA 2025-02-24.
- (Maya Chen) Create an automated node health check that flags nodes with repeated fsync/disk sync stalls exposing metric: node_disk_sync_latency_p95 > 500ms for 5m. Playbook to cordon/drain automatically. ETA 2025-02-28.
- (Lena Rodriguez) Work with cloud provider to increase API attach/detach rate limits or request burst quota; open ticket and track (Cloud-Ticket-777). ETA 2025-03-10.
- (Infra) Add kernel-level mitigation knobs to cluster boot images (tune vm.dirty_* defaults) behind a feature flag; test in staging. ETA 2025-03-14.

Runbook / playbook updates (draft):
- New section: "Detecting fsync/blocking disk stalls"
  - Metrics to watch: node_disk_sync_latency_p95, kubelet_pod_restart_rate, apiserver_watch_latency, scheduler_queue_depth.
  - Immediate steps when node_disk_sync_latency_p95 > 500ms for >5m:
    1. Identify pods on node: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
    2. Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
    3. Drain non-critical pods: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
    4. If node count low, schedule replacement nodes before draining to maintain capacity.
  - Probe tweak guidance: for stateful/backend services, set timeoutSeconds >= 3 and initialDelaySeconds >= 15 unless you have explicit low-latency storage guarantees.

Questions / open items:
- Is there a way to make kubelet probe behavior more tolerant of transient fsync stalls without requiring app-level probe changes? (Investigate kubelet probe grace window or probe aggregation behavior.)
- Should we change our instance family selection policy to avoid NVMe firmware families with known background flush pathologies? Add a gating check in infra repo.

Follow-ups for postmortem (owner assigned):
- Detailed perf tests emulating fsync-heavy workloads on candidate instance types (Infra + Applied ML) — Samir, due 2025-02-28.
- Update deployment lint rules in developer-experience repo to flag probe timeouts under 2s for services that use fsync semantics — Owen, due 2025-02-24.
- Add a synthetic probe that intentionally stresses local disk syncs to our chaos experiments (SRE-runbook/chaos). Lena, due 2025-03-05.

Notes to oncall and next steps if this recurs:
- If you see a small cluster of identical fsync latency warnings, cordon and drain the node ASAP and mark it for firmware check/replacement.
- Prefer increasing probe timeouts as first mitigation for customer-facing services; avoid mass restarting nodes unless disk metrics confirm hardware level faults.

Appendix (commands & snippets):
- Check node fsync warnings:
  ssh node && sudo journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i -E "fsync|sync_file_range|writeback" | tail -n 50
- Check kernel writeback stats:
  cat /proc/meminfo | grep -i Dirty
  sudo sysctl vm.dirty_ratio vm.dirty_background_ratio vm.dirty_expire_centisecs
- Example patch to relax probe timeouts (see above kubectl patch example).

End of notes.

(Will convert to formal postmortem after follow-ups complete.)
